def: How much of an occupation's task content a technology could in principle perform. A measure of potential, not of job loss or timing.
Studying technology through the tasks inside jobs rather than whole occupations; most jobs mix tasks machines can and cannot do.
Automation moves tasks from labour to capital (displacement); new tasks in which people have the edge move work back (reinstatement).
The part of national or business income paid to workers, including an estimate for the self-employed in most official series.
The difference between growth in output per hour and growth in workers' real pay. Its size depends on which worker, which pay and which price index.
The decades of Britain's industrial revolution when output per worker rose much faster than real wages.
The share of people aged 25 to 54 who are working or looking for work; it sidesteps ageing and schooling effects.
David Shapiro's framework for an economy in which machines do most production and household income shifts from wages to ownership and transfers, alongside a rebalancing of power.
Shapiro's name for the separation of economic output from human labour, and of household income from wages.
Shapiro's term for the cross-partisan belief that human labour must be preserved as an economic necessity, a virtue or an identity.
The movement Shapiro launched in December 2025 to end obligatory, not voluntary, work by broadening ownership.
A household's capacity to secure its own living. Shapiro's proposed Economic Agency Index splits household income into wages, property returns and transfers.
In Labor Zero, a household's recurring ownership income divided by its wages plus transfers. A CAR of 4 means 80% of that income comes from capital.
In Labor Zero, the share of household resources that arrives through qualifying shared institutions such as public wealth funds.
Shapiro's five tiers of post-labor household income, from universal programmes at the base to residual wages at the top.
Shapiro's five layers of a new social contract, meant to give citizens leverage once labour no longer does.
A future in which owners of digital platforms and machines extract rents from everyone else. Shapiro calls it the default path without new institutions.
A regular cash payment to every individual, without a means test or work requirement.
A cash floor for those below a threshold; most US pilots of the 2020s are guaranteed-income trials rather than universal ones.
An income floor delivered through the tax system that shrinks gradually as earnings rise.
A US wage subsidy paid through the tax system to low-income working families; the closest thing to a negative income tax actually enacted, but tied to work.
A regular payment to every resident from the returns on a commonly owned asset, such as Alaska's Permanent Fund Dividend.
A state-owned investment fund. Norway's invests oil revenue abroad and funds the budget; Alaska's also pays residents directly.
A one-off endowment of wealth to every person, often at birth or adulthood. Baby bonds are a means-tested version.
Workers holding shares in the firm that employs them, in the US often through an employee stock ownership plan.
The proposal to treat the data people generate as work deserving payment, rather than a free by-product captured by platforms.
Free or subsidised public services, such as housing, transport and digital access, delivered to everyone as of right.
A public offer of paid work to anyone who wants it, usually at a set wage.
Extra local economic activity generated per dollar of cash transferred, including spillovers to people who got nothing.
Shapiro's two attractors for a post-labor future: shared, ecological abundance or elite-captured high tech amid low living standards.
Shapiro's term for paid work that people keep choosing humans for: attention, presence and accountable roles.
